Threat.value: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

vignette:
Eleanor had spent most of her adult life moving briskly through courthouses, jails, and cramped interview rooms as a public defender, a woman accustomed to reading faces, listening for shifts in tone, and walking alone from the parking lot to her office after long days. At 78, she was still married and still working part time, proud of the steadiness she had maintained over the years. The assault happened late one winter afternoon after she left a client meeting and crossed a nearly empty lot behind the county building. A man came up fast from behind, close enough that she felt the shock of his presence before she fully understood it, and in the confusion of being grabbed and shoved, she knew only the violence of it, the loss of control, and the fact that the world around her had gone suddenly unsafe. In the weeks that followed, she found herself turning her head again and again when she was outside, looking behind her before unlocking the car, before stepping from the curb, before reaching for her front door. The habit appeared first in the places that had once felt routine: the courthouse garage, the grocery store parking lot, the path from her office to the elevator. She said she could not stop herself from checking whether someone was there, and if she saw a man walking even a little too close behind her, her body tightened immediately and she hurried away, certain that she needed to know where he was at all times.

At work, Eleanor noticed herself watching people more closely than she used to. In meetings, she studied the men who stood in doorways or sat too near the exit, not because anything specific had happened but because their movements now seemed important in a way they had not before. She found herself tracking hands, posture, and distance, trying to decide who might be harmless and who might suddenly turn on her. This was especially hard in the public defender's office, where clients, court officers, and strangers came and went through the same narrow hallways. She would catch herself focusing on a man's expression as he approached her desk, or on whether someone in the corridor was looking at her too long, and the effort left her feeling tired and on edge. Her husband noticed that she no longer wanted to walk to dinner after dark, and that in public she tended to drift slightly behind him so she could see who was around them. Even at home, when the doorbell rang, she would stand very still for a moment, listening and watching the entryway before moving.

What unsettled Eleanor most was how easily she startled. A phone ringing beside her, a sudden voice in the office, the clatter of a dropped tray in a restaurant, or the quick approach of someone from behind could make her jump before she could think. She described the feeling as if her whole body had become too alert, always braced for something to happen. Sometimes the reaction embarrassed her, especially when it occurred in front of colleagues or her husband, but it also confirmed for her that the world could change without warning. She began choosing seats with her back to a wall and avoided being cornered in crowded places, not out of any desire to be difficult but because she felt she needed to keep herself positioned where she could see what was coming. Over time, these habits narrowed the way she moved through the day. She was still working, but she arranged her schedule to avoid late returns to the office, and she relied more often on her husband to accompany her on errands.

Eleanor came for help when she realized how much energy she was spending each day scanning, checking, and staying ready for danger, even in places she had once trusted. The assault had occurred months earlier, but she still felt most comfortable only when she knew exactly who was near her and could see them clearly. She was not asking to forget what happened; what she hoped for was to stop feeling as though every stranger, every footstep behind her, and every sudden sound might mean another attack was about to begin.
